q: Trace the Wente Chardonnay selection — where it came from, and why it matters.
accept: ernest wente planted it at livermore in 1912 from french cuttings via the university
livermore 1912 the heritage selection behind most california chardonnay
wente selection predates the dijon clones and gives millerandage and low yields
1912 livermore planting propagated as budwood across california
ans: Ernest Wente planted Chardonnay in the Livermore Valley in 1912, from cuttings obtained through the University of California from French material of Montpellier origin. Wente propagated it and sold budwood for decades, at a time when almost nobody else in California had any Chardonnay at all. The 'Wente selection' — actually a family of heritage selections rather than one clone — is marked by small, uneven, millerandage-prone clusters: low yields, high skin-to-juice ratio, concentrated flavour, and historically a heavy virus load that later cleanup programmes at FPS addressed. It is the genetic backbone of essentially all California Chardonnay planted before the Dijon clones arrived in the 1980s, and growers still choose it for texture over the more uniform Dijon material. Livermore's other legacy is Cresta Blanca's Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, from Château d'Yquem cuttings brought over by Charles Wetmore in the 1880s.
exp: When a producer says 'old-vine California Chardonnay' or 'heritage selection', this is what they mean; Stony Hill and much of the classicist lineage trace back to Wente budwood. The practical point for tasting is that hens-and-chickens clusters concentrate flavour and lower yields — the plant material itself is doing part of what winemakers get credit for.

q: Explain smoke taint: how it gets into the wine, why a sample that tastes clean can still fail, and what a producer can do about it.
accept: volatile phenols like guaiacol bind as glycosides and are released by saliva
smoke phenols absorbed after veraison bind to sugars so a clean nose can finish ashy
testing must measure bound glycosides as well as free guaiacol
minimise skin contact press whole clusters or declassify the fruit entirely
ans: Wildfire smoke carries volatile phenols — guaiacol, 4-methylguaiacol, cresols and syringol among them — which are absorbed through the skins and leaves, with the vine most vulnerable from véraison onward. The vine then conjugates them to sugars as non-volatile glycosides. Those are odourless and tasteless in the glass, which is the trap: enzymes in saliva cleave them in the mouth, so a wine can smell clean, taste fine on entry and finish ashy, drying and like a wet ashtray, and can get worse in bottle as hydrolysis continues. Any credible analysis therefore measures both free and bound forms, not free phenols alone. Mitigation is about keeping phenols in the skins and out of the wine: pick early, press whole clusters fast, avoid maceration and hard press fractions, no extended skin contact, consider flash détente or reverse osmosis over a phenolic-stripping resin, and bleed off rosé or sparkling base instead of red. The last option is the honest one — decline the fruit and make nothing.
exp: 2020 is the reference vintage: the August lightning complex fires and the late-September Glass Fire led numerous Napa and Sonoma estates to declassify, sell off or simply not bottle red wine. Whites and sparkling bases pressed straight off the skins came through far better, which is itself the clearest demonstration that the compounds live in the skin. The candidate's takeaway is that 'we tasted it and it was fine' is not a defensible answer.

q: Walk the press fractions of a 4,000 kg marc.
ans: Cuvée: first 2,050 L; taille: next 500 L; rebêche beyond to distillation
exp: The 4,000 kg 'marc' is the legal pressing unit — numbers the oral loves.

q: Define 'liqueur d'expédition' precisely and give the Brut Nature condition.
accept: dosage wine plus sugar brut nature none added
expedition liqueur dosage zero for brut nature
ans: The post-disgorgement topping liqueur (wine ± sugar) setting dosage; Brut Nature adds none (0–3 g/L residual only)
exp: The same wine may top itself — 'dosage zéro' houses use reserve wine alone.

q: Name the four towns of the medieval Champagne fairs — the medieval commerce answer.
ans: Troyes, Provins, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube — the Counts of Champagne's fair towns
exp: Master orals reach into history: six fairs a year across four towns made the region rich before the wine did.

q: Explain 'échelle' pricing's death and what replaced it.
accept: free contract negotiation replaced percentile pricing 1990
ans: The CIVC's fixed price-per-kilo × village percentage ended (1990); free grower-house contracts replaced it, cru labels surviving as prestige markers
exp: Grand cru on a label today is geography, not a paycheck.

q: Which house holds the deepest reserve-wine library ('la réserve perpétuelle' claims aside) and pioneered oak-fermented NV at scale?
ans: Krug (Grande Cuvée blends 120+ wines across 10+ years; all base wines in small oak)
exp: Bollinger's magnum reserve library is the rival answer — argue either with evidence.

q: What did the 1911 Champagne riots decide?
ans: The delimitation fight — Aube growers rioted over exclusion; 1927 law finally fixed the zone including the Aube
exp: Marne cellars burned; the boundary is written in that fire.

q: Name the single-vineyard Champagne that started the lieu-dit era in 1935.
exp: 5.83 ha of 45° south slope — the site that made 'terroir Champagne' arguable.

q: Give varietal and village for Krug's Clos d'Ambonnay.
ans: 100% Pinot Noir from a 0.68 ha walled plot in Ambonnay
exp: Blanc de Noirs at Clos du Mesnil pricing squared.

q: What is 'gyropalette' throughput versus hand riddling?
ans: Machine riddling: ~1 week in 504-bottle cages vs ~6 weeks by hand on pupitres
exp: Invented in Catalonia (girasol) for Cava — a cross-region oral favorite.

accept: shallow broad basket press for whole clusters
ans: The traditional shallow vertical basket press — whole clusters, gentle fractions, the classic Champagne press
exp: Its geometry keeps black skins off white juice.

q: The legal minimum potential alcohol and maximum yield questions: give the standard harvest yield cap.
accept: around 10400 kilograms per hectare set annually
ans: ~10,400 kg/ha as the base cap, adjusted annually by the Comité (plus reserve mechanisms)
exp: Yield politics move with global demand — the answer is 'set annually', with the number in hand.

q: Name three universally declared modern Champagne vintages and one notorious skip.
exp: 2008's late-declared releases are the connoisseur's current chase.

q: Explain climate change's effect on Champagne's dosage and picking dates.
accept: riper base wine lower dosage earlier harvest
ans: Riper base wines have driven dosages steadily downward (Brut Nature's rise) and harvests weeks earlier than mid-century norms
exp: Chaptalization is now less needed — an unthinkable sentence in 1980.

q: Explain yeast autolysis: what physically happens, on what timescale, and what it contributes to the wine.
accept: dead yeast cells self digest and release mannoproteins and amino acids
enzymatic breakdown of the yeast cell giving polysaccharides texture and toast notes
autolysis releases mannoproteins for foam stability and amino acids for brioche
cell walls degrade over years giving creamier texture and maillard aromas
ans: Once the second fermentation finishes, the yeast dies and its own hydrolytic enzymes — proteases, glucanases — digest the cell from within, and the cell wall progressively releases mannoproteins and other polysaccharides, amino acids, peptides and nucleotides into the wine. Breakdown begins within months, but meaningful sensory change is measured in years: the legal 12 months on lees is a floor, and the brioche, toast and hazelnut character candidates describe generally needs three years and well beyond. What it gives is threefold. Mannoproteins stabilise the foam, so the bead is finer and more persistent and the texture creamier. Amino acids and nucleotides feed Maillard-type aromas and add savoury depth. And the lees are reductive, consuming oxygen, so a bottle that has spent a decade sur lattes can arrive at disgorgement startlingly fresh — then age quickly once that cushion is removed, which is precisely the argument behind late disgorgement.
exp: This is the reason the minimum ageing law exists at all, and the reason an RD or late-disgorged bottle tastes younger than its vintage suggests — the clock effectively starts at disgorgement. It also explains why poignettage and lees contact practices matter to producers chasing texture rather than aroma.
